common_name: Dr. Potter Pawpaw (Reliable Late-Season Indiana Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5-7.0) soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; plant alongside a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar, since two are needed for reliable cross-pollination and fruit set.

directions: Dr. Potter is a wild-tree selection documented from Julietta, Indiana, and cataloged among Kentucky State University's historic pawpaw cultivar records. The fruit runs on the small side with rich, deep-yellow flesh and a mild, gently sweet flavor, and it holds up well after picking compared to many softer-fleshed pawpaws. It ripens late in the season and, like all pawpaws, needs a genetically distinct second tree nearby for pollination and fruit set.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

directions: Buckman is an older named pawpaw selection distinguished by unusually pale, white-toned flesh rather than the yellow-orange color typical of most cultivars, paired with a mild flavor. It is a late to very-late ripening selection, extending the harvest window for growers who also plant earlier cultivars. Buckman survives today mainly in historical cultivar records rather than wide commercial distribution, and like other pawpaws it requires a genetically distinct second tree for cross-pollination.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

directions: Kurle originated in Michigan as a seedling selection from the Davis pawpaw line, one of breeder Corwin Davis's influential mid-20th-century wild selections. Fruit is small to medium in size with yellow flesh and yellow skin, similar in character to its Davis parentage. Like other named pawpaws, Kurle needs cross-pollination from a genetically distinct second tree to set a reliable crop.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

directions: Fairchild is a named seedling selection of the Ohio cultivar Ketter, sharing some of that parent's rich flavor while ripening earlier in the season. It is documented in Kentucky State University's historical pawpaw cultivar records among the many named selections that arose from open-pollinated Ketter seed. As with all pawpaws, Fairchild needs a genetically distinct second tree nearby for pollination, since it will not reliably set fruit on its own.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

directions: Silver Creek is a wild-tree selection documented from Millstadt, Illinois, and cataloged among Kentucky State University's historical pawpaw cultivar records. It produces medium-sized fruit and represents the many regionally significant heirloom pawpaw selections that circulated among enthusiasts before the modern KSU and Peterson breeding programs. Plant it alongside a genetically distinct second pawpaw tree, since cross-pollination is required for fruit set.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

directions: Little Rosie is a named pawpaw selection documented from Evansville, Indiana, notable chiefly for its small fruit size relative to most named cultivars. It remains part of the historical record of regional wild-tree selections that Kentucky State University has cataloged alongside better-known Indiana cultivars such as Overleese. A genetically distinct second pawpaw tree is required nearby, as Little Rosie will not reliably set fruit on its own.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

directions: Rees is an older named pawpaw selection noted in Kentucky State University's historical cultivar records for its pale-yellow flesh, good flavor, and notably small seeds relative to most pawpaws, a trait that increases the proportion of edible flesh per fruit. Exact origin and ripening timing were not well documented when the selection was first cataloged, but it remains of interest to collectors seeking low-seed heirloom genetics. A genetically distinct second tree is required nearby for cross-pollination and fruit set.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

directions: Hope's August is a named pawpaw selection documented from Paint, Ohio, valued primarily for its early maturity, ripening ahead of most named cultivars and extending the pawpaw harvest toward late summer. It is one of a small family of related Ohio selections, including the similarly named Hope's September, cataloged in Kentucky State University's historical pawpaw cultivar records. Like all pawpaws, it needs a genetically distinct second tree nearby for pollination since it cannot reliably set fruit alone.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

common_name: Kentucky Legend Pawpaw (Large Firm-Fleshed England's Orchard Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5-7.0) soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; plant alongside a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar, since two are needed for reliable cross-pollination and fruit set.

directions: Kentucky Legend is a pawpaw introduction from England's Orchard and Nursery, the Kentucky nursery behind other named selections including Cantaloupe and Marshmallow. It produces large fruit, often reaching around 13 ounces, with firm-textured flesh and a notably low seed percentage comparable to the classic cultivar Sunflower. Kentucky Legend ripens mid-to-late season and, like other named pawpaws, requires a genetically distinct second tree nearby for cross-pollination.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

directions: Atria is a pawpaw selection introduced by Red Fern Farm, the Iowa permaculture nursery known for its cold-climate fruit and nut selections. It bears large fruit with excellent flavor and a notably low seed count for the species, ripening mid-season. Like other pawpaws, Atria requires a genetically distinct second tree nearby for cross-pollination to set a reliable crop.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

common_name: Horn's White Pawpaw (Unusually Pale-Fleshed Heirloom Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5-7.0) soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; plant alongside a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar, since two are needed for reliable cross-pollination and fruit set.

directions: Horn's White is an heirloom pawpaw selection prized for flesh that is unusually white and creamy rather than the typical yellow-orange, with tasting notes reminiscent of coconut and cherimoya alongside classic banana-custard pawpaw flavor. Fruit runs large, often around 12 ounces, and ripens late in the season. Like all pawpaws, Horn's White needs a genetically distinct second tree nearby for cross-pollination, since it will not reliably set fruit alone.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program
